findings.body: `formatBackupCode` is defined as a `const` arrow function at line 163, but it is referenced inside `handleSetup` at line 95 (`body.backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)`). Because `handleSetup` is only *called* later (after render), the closure captures the variable binding, and by the time it runs the `const` has been initialized — so this works at runtime due to JavaScript closure semantics over the function-scoped `const` in the same render pass. However, this is fragile and confusing: if `handleSetup` were ever called during the same render before line 163 executes (it cannot be, since it's an event handler), it would throw a TDZ error. More practically, the function is re-created every render and the dependency is implicit. This should be moved above `handleSetup` or extracted to module scope for clarity and to avoid subtle bugs if the component is refactored.

findings.title: Object URL for backup codes download is revoked while the download link may still be in use, and is never revoked on unmount
findings.body: At line 98-99, `URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)` is called before creating a new URL, which is correct for replacing a previous blob. However, the blob URL is stored in state and used by the `<a download href={backupCodesUrl}>` link at line 283. If the user clicks download, then starts a *new* setup flow (which calls `handleSetup` again), the old URL is revoked — but the new URL replaces it, so the link is fine. The real leak: when the component unmounts or the modal is closed without downloading, `backupCodesUrl` is never revoked, leaking the blob URL (and the in-memory blob containing all backup codes) until the page is unloaded. `resetState` (line 71-75) does not revoke the URL. This should revoke the URL in a cleanup effect or in `resetState`.

findings.title: After enabling 2FA, the modal shows backup codes but `onEnable` is only called on manual close, leaving the parent UI stale
findings.body: When `handleEnable` succeeds (line 134-137), the step is set to `DisplayBackupCodes` but `onEnable()` is NOT called — it is deferred until the user clicks the 'close' button (line 266-270). This means the parent component (the security settings page) does not update its state (e.g. the 2FA toggle switch) until the user manually closes the modal. If the user closes the modal via the dialog's X button or by clicking outside (the `onOpenChange` handler), `onEnable` is never called, and the parent UI will show 2FA as disabled even though it is now enabled on the server. The `onOpenChange` prop is passed to `Dialog` at line 166 but there is no logic to call `onEnable` or `resetState` when the dialog is dismissed. This is a state-synchronization bug that will confuse users and could lead to them attempting to re-enable 2FA.

findings.title: Component is named `TwoFactor` instead of `BackupCode`, and has no autoFocus prop unlike its sibling
findings.body: The default export is `function TwoFactor({ center = true })` but the file is `BackupCode.tsx` and it is imported as `BackupCode`. This is a copy-paste error from `TwoFactor.tsx` and will confuse developers and any tooling that relies on component names (e.g. React DevTools, error stack traces). Additionally, unlike `TwoFactor` which gained an `autoFocus` prop in this PR, `BackupCode` always renders without autofocus management, so when the user switches to the backup code input on the login page the field is not focused, hurting usability.

findings.title: minLength/maxLength validation does not match the actual code format and allows invalid submissions
findings.body: The input has `minLength={10}` (comment says 'without dash') and `maxLength={11}` ('with dash'). The stored codes are 10 hex characters; the UI formats them as `XXXXX-XXXXX` (11 chars). But the server strips ALL dashes with `replaceAll("-", "")`, so a user could enter `XXXXX-XXXXX` (11 chars, valid) or `XXXXXXXXXX` (10 chars, valid). However, `minLength={10}` would also accept `XXXXX-XXXX` (10 chars with a dash in the wrong place) which after stripping becomes 9 characters and will never match. The validation is purely length-based and does not enforce the hex format or the dash position. This leads to confusing 'incorrect backup code' errors for malformed input. The input should validate the pattern `^[0-9a-fA-F]{5}-?[0-9a-fA-F]{5}$` or normalize on submit.

findings.title: Switching between TOTP and backup code does not clear the other field's value, allowing both to be submitted
findings.body: When the user toggles between TOTP and backup code via the 'Lost access' / 'Go back' buttons (lines 103-133), the code clears the field being switched *away from* (e.g. switching to backup code clears `totpCode` at line 125, switching back clears `backupCode` at line 109). However, react-hook-form's `setValue` does not trigger re-render of the hidden input's `value` attribute in all cases, and more importantly the `onSubmit` sends `...values` which includes ALL form values. If the user types a TOTP code, then switches to backup code, types a backup code, the `totpCode` value may still be present in the form state (the `setValue("totpCode", "")` at line 125 should clear it, but the hidden input at TwoFactor.tsx line 33 uses `value={value}` from local state, not the form value — so the form's `totpCode` and the local `value` can diverge). On the server side (next-auth-options.ts line 131), the check is `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` — if both `totpCode` and `backupCode` are non-empty, the backup code branch wins and the TOTP is ignored, which is probably fine, but if the user switches back and forth the stale values can cause unexpected behavior. The form should use `unregister` or `resetField` when switching modes to ensure only one second-factor value is ever submitted.

findings.title: Zod schema makes password optional when `totpEmail` is present, but backup code flow still requires password field to be absent
findings.body: The schema at line 63 sets `password: !!totpEmail ? z.literal("") : z.string().min(1, ...)`. This means when arriving via the TOTP JWT flow (`totpEmail` set), the password must be an empty string. However, the backup code flow is reached *after* the initial password login (the user enters email+password, gets `SecondFactorRequired`, then enters a backup code). In that flow `totpEmail` is null, so the password field is required by the schema — but the password input is hidden (line 193: `{ hidden: twoFactorRequired }`). The form still submits the password value from the initial login (it's in the form state), so this works, but it's fragile: if the password field is unmounted when `twoFactorRequired` becomes true, react-hook-form may unregister it and the value is lost, causing a schema validation error on submit. The schema should explicitly allow the password to be optional/passthrough when `twoFactorRequired` is true, not just when `totpEmail` is set.

findings.title: E2E test uses `prisma` without importing it, and backup code login/disable flows are not tested
findings.body: The test file references `prisma?.user.findFirst` at lines 64 and 141 but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` at the top of the file (the imports at lines 1-8 only include `@playwright/test`, `otplib`, `@calcom/lib/crypto`, `@calcom/lib/totp`, and `./lib/fixtures`). This will cause a `ReferenceError` at runtime when the test executes, meaning the 'Login with 2FA enabled' and 'Disable 2FA' steps will fail. Additionally, the PR description says 'enable their use during 2fa login flow' and 'fix 2fa setup test to include new backup code screen', but the only new test coverage is for the backup codes *display* (download/copy/close buttons at lines 110-125). There are no tests for: logging in with a backup code, the 'Lost access' toggle on the login page, disabling 2FA with a backup code, or that a used backup code cannot be reused. The TODO at line 12 acknowledges this, but the PR claims to 'enable their use during 2fa login flow' without proving it works.

findings.title: The 'Lost access' toggle button in the disable modal does not clear the password field, and the toggle button lacks a `type="button"`
findings.body: The 'Lost access' / 'Go back' button at lines 113-121 calls `resetForm(false)` which clears `backupCode` and `totpCode` but intentionally keeps the password (the `clearPassword = false` argument). This is probably intentional so the user doesn't have to retype their password when toggling. However, the button is inside a `<Form>` (line 91) and does not have `type="button"` — it defaults to `type="submit"`, which will trigger form submission (calling `handleDisable`) when the user only intended to toggle the input mode. This is a real bug: clicking 'Lost access' will submit the form with whatever values are currently present, likely resulting in an error or an unintended disable attempt. The button needs `type="button"`.

findings.title: The 'Continue' button on the password step has both `type="submit"` and an `onClick={handleSetup}`, causing double submission
findings.body: The button at lines 232-240 is inside a `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable} form={form}>` (line 209) but also has `onClick={handleSetup}` (line 236) and `type="submit"` (line 234). The `handleSetup` function (line 77) calls `e.preventDefault()`, so the form's native submit is prevented, but the `Form` component's `handleSubmit` wrapper may still fire `handleEnable` with the current (empty) form values. This can cause `handleEnable` to run with an empty `totpCode`, which will fail server-side with `IncorrectTwoFactorCode` and set an error message, or worse, race with `handleSetup`. The button should either be `type="button"` with only `onClick={handleSetup}`, or the `handleSetup` should be wired through the form's submit handler properly. The current setup is confusing and error-prone.

findings.title: Backup code consumption uses a non-atomic read-modify-write, allowing the same code to be replayed concurrently
findings.body: When a valid backup code is used at login, the code is invalidated by setting `backupCodes[index] = null` and then calling `prisma.user.update` (lines 148-156). This is a classic read-modify-write race: two concurrent login requests with the same backup code will both read the same `backupCodes` array (both see the code as present), both find `index !== -1`, and both proceed to update the user record. The second update overwrites the first, but both requests have already passed validation and will both create a valid session. This means a single backup code can be replayed concurrently to create multiple sessions. The fix is to use an atomic conditional update, e.g. `UPDATE users SET backupCodes = <new array> WHERE id = <id> AND backupCodes = <old encrypted value>` and check the affected row count, or use a database transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

findings.title: Setup endpoint overwrites existing backup codes and TOTP secret without checking if 2FA is already in progress, enabling secret fixation
findings.body: The setup endpoint checks `if (user.twoFactorEnabled)` at line 42 and rejects if already enabled. But if a user has previously started setup (secret and backup codes stored, `twoFactorEnabled: false`) and starts again, the endpoint unconditionally generates a new secret and new backup codes and overwrites the old ones (lines 58-72). This is mostly fine, but consider: an attacker who has temporarily compromised a user's session (e.g. via XSS) could call this endpoint to regenerate the TOTP secret and backup codes, then read the new secret and backup codes from the response, effectively locking out the legitimate user and gaining persistent access. The endpoint requires the user's password (line 51), which mitigates this, but if the session is compromised and the password is known or cached, this is a risk. More importantly, there is no invalidation of the previous secret — if the user had already configured their authenticator app with the old secret, it will silently stop working. The endpoint should either reject if a secret already exists (requiring explicit reset) or clearly warn the user.

findings.title: Backup code instructions text says 'Each backup code can be used exactly once' but the disable flow deletes all codes without consuming the used one
findings.body: The locale string `backup_code_instructions` says: 'Each backup code can be used exactly once to grant access without your authenticator.' This is shown both during setup (as the description for the DisplayBackupCodes step) and as the label for the backup code input field. However, the disable-2FA flow (disable.ts) does not consume the individual code — it validates it and then deletes ALL backup codes. So the statement 'each backup code can be used exactly once' is misleading in the context of disabling 2FA: the code is used once to disable 2FA, but that action also destroys all other codes. The text should clarify that using a backup code to sign in consumes only that code, but disabling 2FA removes all remaining codes. Alternatively, the disable flow should only consume the used code and leave the others (though since 2FA is being disabled, deleting all is reasonable — the text just shouldn't overpromise).

findings.body: The download link at lines 283-287 is ``. Nesting a `

findings.title: Backup code branch is reachable for users whose identity provider is not CAL, bypassing the ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled check
findings.body: At line 113, the check `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode)` throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled`. This means a Google/SAML user can proceed past this check if they supply a `totpCode`. The backup code branch at line 131 is `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` — it does not check `credentials.totpCode` and does not check the identity provider. So a Google/SAML user with 2FA enabled could submit a `backupCode` (without a `totpCode`) and reach the backup code validation. This may be intentional (backup codes are a fallback for all 2FA users), but it's inconsistent with the TOTP path which explicitly requires `totpCode` for non-CAL users. If backup codes are meant to be CAL-only (since setup.ts line 34 rejects non-CAL users from setting up 2FA), then a non-CAL user should never have backup codes, and this branch should also verify `user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL` or at least that `user.backupCodes` exists (which it does at line 137). The current code would throw `MissingBackupCodes` for non-CAL users without backup codes, which is fine, but the logic is convoluted and could mask misconfiguration.
